claim: Mammalian myocardium safeguards its ATP set-point despite 10-fold fluctuations in cardiac workload.
source: In particular, mammalian myocardium exquisitely safeguards its ATP set-point despite 10-fold fluctuations in cardiac workload.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ATP homeostasis in the heart.

claim: Mitoflashes negatively regulate ATP production in isolated respiring mitochondria.
source: Specifically, mitoflashes negatively regulate ATP production in isolated respiring mitochondria and, their activity waxes and wanes to counteract the ATP supply-demand imbalance caused by superfluous substrate and altered workload in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that inhibiting mitoflashes increases ATP production in isolated mitochondria (Figure 1).

claim: Mitoflash activity waxes and wanes to counteract ATP supply-demand imbalance caused by superfluous substrate and altered workload in cardiomyocytes.
source: Specifically, mitoflashes negatively regulate ATP production in isolated respiring mitochondria and, their activity waxes and wanes to counteract the ATP supply-demand imbalance caused by superfluous substrate and altered workload in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing mitoflash responses to substrate changes and electrical pacing (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Manipulating mitoflash activity is sufficient to inversely shift the otherwise stable ATP set-point.
source: Moreover, manipulating mitoflash activity is sufficient to inversely shift the otherwise stable ATP set-point.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that inhibiting mitoflashes with antioxidants or SOD2 overexpression increases ATP levels (Figure 4).

claim: Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATP synthase mediates the coupling between mitoflash production and ATP set-point regulation.
source: Mechanistically, the Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATP synthase appears to mediate the coupling between mitoflash production and ATP set-point regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Bcl-xL manipulation affects both mitoflash frequency and ATP levels (Figure 5).

claim: Mitoflashes constitute a digital auto-regulator for ATP homeostasis in the heart.
source: These findings indicate mitoflashes appear to constitute a digital auto-regulator for ATP homeostasis in the heart.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental findings showing mitoflashes meet criteria for ATP set-point regulation.

claim: ATP is the most important energy currency and mitochondria supply ATP at a rate of ~6 kg/day in the human heart.
source: ATP is the most important energy currency and mitochondria constitute the largest cellular powerhouse, supplying ATP at a rate of ~6 kg/day in the human heart (Neubauer, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Neubauer, 2007.

claim: The rate of energy consumption and supply augments by 5-10 folds during fight-or-flight or exercise, but the ATP concentration remains remarkably constant.
source: An exemplary case is found in mammalian myocardium - the rate of energy consumption and supply (i.e., ATP flux) augments by 5–10 folds in situations of fight-or-flight or exercise, but the ATP concentration (i.e., ATP set-point) remains remarkably constant (Balaban et al., 1986; Neely et al., 1973; Matthews et al., 1981; Allue et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ADP, Pi and Ca2+ have been suggested to be regulators of ATP homeostasis, but challenges exist.
source: ADP, Pi and Ca2+ have been suggested to be regulators of ATP homeostasis, but challenges exist because of the relative constancy of ADP and Pi (Katz et al., 1989; Yaniv et al., 2010; Balaban, 2012) and the extremely low activity of the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter (MCU) in cardiac myocytes (Fieni et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MCU is dispensable for energy metabolism except under extreme physiological stress.
source: Moreover, recent findings in MCU knockout mice suggest that MCU is dispensable for energy metabolism except under extreme physiological stress (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2013.

claim: Myocardial overexpression of dominant negative MCU increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption due in part to secondary effect on cytosol Ca2+ homeostasis.
source: Myocardial overexpression of the dominant negative MCU increases, rather than decreases, mitochondrial oxygen consumption due in part to secondary effect on cytosol Ca2+ homeostasis (Rasmussen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rasmussen et al., 2015.

claim: Mitoflash has been ubiquitously detected in all eukaryotic species examined, from C. elegans to zebrafish and to rodents and humans.
source: Mitochondrial flash (mitoflash) represents a recently discovered dynamic activity of the mitochondria (Wang et al., 2008) and has been ubiquitously detected in all eukaryotic species examined, from C. elegans to zebrafish and to rodents and humans (Wang et al., 2008; Hou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016a; Shen et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Individual mitoflash consists of multiple signal components including bursting superoxide production, transient matrix alkalization, oxidative redox shift, transient depletion of NADH and FADH2, and mitochondrial membrane potential depolarization.
source: Individual mitoflash consists of multiple signal components including bursting superoxide production, transient matrix alkalization, oxidative redox shift, transient depletion of the electron donors NADH and FADH2, and mitochondrial membrane potential depolarization (Wang et al., 2008, 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The generation of mitoflashes in intact cells requires the integrity of the electron transfer chain.
source: The generation of mitoflashes in intact cells requires the integrity of the electron transfer chain (ETC) (Wang et al., 2008); and mitoflash frequency is highly regulated over a wide dynamic range by factors including metabolic state, thus the mitoflash activity is considered a biomarker for mitochondrial energy metabolism under certain conditions (Wei et al., 2011; Pouvreau, 2010; Fang et al., 2011; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Mitoflash frequency is highly regulated over a wide dynamic range by factors including metabolic state.
source: The generation of mitoflashes in intact cells requires the integrity of the electron transfer chain (ETC) (Wang et al., 2008); and mitoflash frequency is highly regulated over a wide dynamic range by factors including metabolic state, thus the mitoflash activity is considered a biomarker for mitochondrial energy metabolism under certain conditions (Wei et al., 2011; Pouvreau, 2010; Fang et al., 2011; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Protons produced by photolysis or electroneutral proton ionophores act as a powerful mitoflash trigger.
source: Most recently, we have shown that protons produced by photolysis or electroneutral proton ionophores act as a powerful mitoflash trigger (Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016b.

claim: Mitoflash events occurred randomly at a rate of 26 ± 2 events / (1000 µm2·100s) in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: We found that mitoflash events occurred randomly at a rate of 26 ± 2 events / (1000 µm2·100s) (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Individual mitoflashes exhibited an average rise time of 7 s, peak amplitude of 0.5 (ΔF/F0), and duration of 22 s in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: individual mitoflashes exhibited an average rise time of 7 s, peak amplitude of 0.5 (ΔF/F0), and duration of 22 s, comparable with those in intact cardiac myocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SS31 decreased mitoflash frequency by 44% in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: Treatments using the mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, SS31 and mitoTEMPO, or the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) inhibitor cyclosporin A (CsA) decreased the mitoflash frequency by 44%, 31%, and 47% (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: MitoTEMPO decreased mitoflash frequency by 31% in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: Treatments using the mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, SS31 and mitoTEMPO, or the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) inhibitor cyclosporin A (CsA) decreased the mitoflash frequency by 44%, 31%, and 47% (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Cyclosporin A decreased mitoflash frequency by 47% in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: Treatments using the mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, SS31 and mitoTEMPO, or the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) inhibitor cyclosporin A (CsA) decreased the mitoflash frequency by 44%, 31%, and 47% (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: SS31 enhanced the rate of ATP production by 25% in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: Parallel luciferin luminescence measurement showed that, along with the repression of mitoflash activity, the rate of ATP production, assessed as the cumulative ATP formation over a 5 min time window, was enhanced by 25%, 24%, and 22%, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MitoTEMPO enhanced the rate of ATP production by 24% in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: Parallel luciferin luminescence measurement showed that, along with the repression of mitoflash activity, the rate of ATP production, assessed as the cumulative ATP formation over a 5 min time window, was enhanced by 25%, 24%, and 22%, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cyclosporin A enhanced the rate of ATP production by 22% in isolated cardiac mitochondria.
source: Parallel luciferin luminescence measurement showed that, along with the repression of mitoflash activity, the rate of ATP production, assessed as the cumulative ATP formation over a 5 min time window, was enhanced by 25%, 24%, and 22%, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All metabolites examined, including glucose, free fatty acid and pyruvate, dose-dependently increased the mitoflash frequency.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, all metabolites examined, including glucose, free fatty acid and pyruvate, dose-dependently increased the mitoflash frequency, consistent with previous reports (Fang et al., 2011; Pouvreau, 2010; Wei et al., 2011; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior research.

claim: 10 mM pyruvate increased the mitoflash frequency by 12 folds comparing to 5.6 mM glucose.
source: Strikingly, 10 mM pyruvate, the immediate metabolite that enters mitochondria and feeds the tricarboxylic cycle, elicited the most vigorous mitoflash activity, increasing the mitoflash frequency by 12 folds comparing to 5.6 mM glucose (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The stimulatory effect of pyruvate on mitoflash activity was fully reversed upon pyruvate washout.
source: This stimulatory effect on mitoflash activity was fully reversed upon pyruvate washout, and was largely prevented by α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid, an inhibitor of the mitochondrial pyruvate transporter (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid largely prevented the stimulatory effect of pyruvate on mitoflash activity.
source: This stimulatory effect on mitoflash activity was fully reversed upon pyruvate washout, and was largely prevented by α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid, an inhibitor of the mitochondrial pyruvate transporter (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Switching from 5.6 mM glucose to 10 mM pyruvate augmented the mitoflash frequency from 1.2 ± 0.3 to 11.5 ± 2.8 mitoflashes / (1000 µm2·100s) in beating hearts under Langendorff perfusion.
source: Likewise, a large and robust mitoflash response was obtained in beating hearts under Langendorff perfusion: switching from 5.6 mM glucose to 10 mM pyruvate augmented the mitoflash frequency from 1.2 ± 0.3 to 11.5 ± 2.8 mitoflashes / (1000 µm2·100s) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The intracellular ATP content and ATP/ADP ratio exhibited an initial overshoot upon the glucose-to-pyruvate switch and returned to baseline in about 100 s.
source: Parallel measurements revealed that the intracellular ATP content (measured with the luciferin luminescence method) and the ATP/ADP ratio (measured with the indicator PercevalHR [Tantama et al., 2013]) exhibited an initial overshoot upon the glucose-to-pyruvate switch and returned to its baseline in about 100 s (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and a citation to Tantama et al., 2013.

claim: The significant rise of mitoflash activity occurred concomitantly with a decline in the ATP transient upon glucose-to-pyruvate switch.
source: Interestingly, the time-course response of mitoflashes showed that the significant rise of mitoflash activity occurred concomitantly with a decline in the ATP transient (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The rate of oxygen consumption was increased in response to pyruvate stimulation despite the constancy of ATP.
source: Along with the high activity of mitoflashes at the steady state, the rate of oxygen consumption and the cellular levels of NADH and FADH2 were all increased despite the constancy of ATP (Figure 2D–2F), indicative of decreased efficiency of ATP synthesis and substantiating the conclusion that mitoflashes negatively regulate ATP production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D-2F.

claim: The cellular levels of NADH and FADH2 were increased in response to pyruvate stimulation despite the constancy of ATP.
source: Along with the high activity of mitoflashes at the steady state, the rate of oxygen consumption and the cellular levels of NADH and FADH2 were all increased despite the constancy of ATP (Figure 2D–2F), indicative of decreased efficiency of ATP synthesis and substantiating the conclusion that mitoflashes negatively regulate ATP production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D-2F.

claim: A single heartbeat consumes ~2% of the cellular ATP.
source: In cardiac myocytes, a single heartbeat consumes ~2% of the cellular ATP (Jacobus, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jacobus, 1985.

claim: Mitoflash activity declined precipitously at the onset of electrical pacing in pyruvate-treated cells.
source: The mitoflash activity in pyruvate-treated cells declined precipitously at the onset of electrical pacing, alongside the onset of intracellular Ca2+ transients and cell shortenings; it was readily restored at the offset of pacing, with the cessation of Ca2+ and contractile responses (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mitoflash frequency was diminished by 45% at 1 Hz pacing.
source: Quantitatively, mitoflash frequency was diminished by 45% at 1 Hz, 69% at 2 Hz, and 80% at 5 Hz pacing (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mitoflash frequency was diminished by 69% at 2 Hz pacing.
source: Quantitatively, mitoflash frequency was diminished by 45% at 1 Hz, 69% at 2 Hz, and 80% at 5 Hz pacing (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mitoflash frequency was diminished by 80% at 5 Hz pacing.
source: Quantitatively, mitoflash frequency was diminished by 45% at 1 Hz, 69% at 2 Hz, and 80% at 5 Hz pacing (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Increasing the workload inhibited rather than stimulated mitoflash activity in cardiomyocytes exposed to physiological 5.6 mM glucose.
source: Similar results were found in cardiomyocytes exposed to physiological 5.6 mM glucose in Tyrode's solution, i.e., increasing the workload inhibited rather than stimulated mitoflash activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The cellular ATP content and ATP/ADP ratio were held constant regardless of pacing at different frequencies.
source: Remarkably, the cellular ATP content and ATP/ADP ratio were held constant regardless of pacing at different frequencies (Figure 3D), substantiating the tightness of the ATP set-point regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: β-adrenergic stimulation with isoproterenol (1 μM) inhibited mitoflash frequency by 70% in pyruvate-treated cells.
source: In this regard, we demonstrated that β-adrenergic stimulation with isoproterenol (ISO, 1 μM), to enhance Ca2+ cycling and thus to increase ATP demand, inhibited mitoflash frequency by 70% in pyruvate-treated cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Brief removal of extracellular Ca2+ (5 mM EGTA in nominal 0 Ca2+ solution) increased mitoflash activity by 48%.
source: In contrast, brief removal of extracellular Ca2+ (5 mM EGTA in nominal 0 Ca2+ solution) increased mitoflash activity by 48% (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The ATP content and ATP/ADP ratio were kept constant under either ISO stimulation or Ca2+ manipulation.
source: Notably, the ATP content and ATP/ADP ratio were kept constant under either ISO stimulation or Ca2+ manipulation (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F and G.

claim: Inhibiting mitoflashes with mitochondria-targeted antioxidants SS31 or mitoTEMPO, or overexpression of SOD2 decreased mitoflash frequency and increased the ATP content in intact cardiac myocytes.
source: To answer this question, we inhibited mitoflashes with mitochondria-targeted antioxidants SS31 or mitoTEMPO, or overexpression of SOD2 in intact cardiac myocytes. As shown in Figure 4A and B, all these manipulations decreased mitoflash frequency and increased the ATP content even in intact cardiac myocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: The ATP set-point was elevated by ~60% while the mitoflash activity was mitigated by ~40% when mitoflashes were inhibited.
source: Quantitatively, the ATP set-point was elevated by ~60% while the mitoflash activity was mitigated by ~40% (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: Linear regression revealed a strong inverse correlation between the mitoflash activity and the cellular ATP content (r = −0.96, p=0.009) at 10 mM pyruvate.
source: Linear regression revealed a strong inverse correlation between the mitoflash activity and the cellular ATP content (r = −0.96, p=0.009) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The proton leakage associated OCR was augmented by 28% in response to 10 mM pyruvate stimulation.
source: Interestingly, we found that the proton leakage associated OCR was augmented by 28% in response to increasing ATP supply, i.e. 10 mM pyruvate stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: ISO treatment attenuated the proton leakage associated OCR by 11%.
source: Increasing workloads by ISO treatment attenuated the proton leakage associated OCR by 11% while decreasing energy expenditure by brief removal of extracellular Ca2+ (5 mM EGTA in nominal 0 Ca2+ solution) elevated the proton leakage associated OCR by 14% (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Brief removal of extracellular Ca2+ (5 mM EGTA in nominal 0 Ca2+ solution) elevated the proton leakage associated OCR by 14%.
source: Increasing workloads by ISO treatment attenuated the proton leakage associated OCR by 11% while decreasing energy expenditure by brief removal of extracellular Ca2+ (5 mM EGTA in nominal 0 Ca2+ solution) elevated the proton leakage associated OCR by 14% (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Inhibition of UCP2 with genipin or RNA interference slightly increased, rather than decreased, the mitoflash incidence.
source: Inhibition of UCP2, the dominant isoform of UCPs in heart (Ricquier and Bouillaud, 2000) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) with either genipin (Zhang et al., 2006) or RNA interference, slightly increased, rather than decreased, the mitoflash incidence (Figure 5A–5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A-5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4, and citations to prior research.

claim: Bcl-xL overexpression markedly decreased mitoflash incidence.
source: Indeed, we found that Bcl-xL overexpression, to inhibit the uncoupled proton flux, markedly decreased mitoflash incidence, whereas knockdown of Bcl-xL with siRNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), increased mitoflashes at both 5.6 mM glucose and 10 mM pyruvate (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Knockdown of Bcl-xL with siRNAs increased mitoflashes at both 5.6 mM glucose and 10 mM pyruvate.
source: Indeed, we found that Bcl-xL overexpression, to inhibit the uncoupled proton flux, markedly decreased mitoflash incidence, whereas knockdown of Bcl-xL with siRNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), increased mitoflashes at both 5.6 mM glucose and 10 mM pyruvate (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Treatment with ABT-737 elevated mitoflash production.
source: Likewise, treatment with ABT-737, a mimetic of BH3-only proteins that inhibits Bcl-xL (Oltersdorf et al., 2005), also elevated mitoflash production (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and a citation to Oltersdorf et al., 2005.

claim: Bcl-xL overexpression caused a 19% upward shift of the ATP set-point.
source: Furthermore, the mitoflash responses were accompanied by a 19% upward shift of the ATP set-point with Bcl-xL overexpression, and an 11% downward shift with ABT-737 treatment (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5F and G.

claim: ABT-737 treatment caused an 11% downward shift of the ATP set-point.
source: Furthermore, the mitoflash responses were accompanied by a 19% upward shift of the ATP set-point with Bcl-xL overexpression, and an 11% downward shift with ABT-737 treatment (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5F and G.

claim: Free protons are short-lived (lifetime ~1.4 ns) and diffuse only over a nanometre scale (~2.1 nm) in the matrix environment.
source: Recent numerical analysis has revealed that free protons are short-lived (lifetime ~1.4 ns) and diffuse only over a nanometre scale (~2.1 nm) in the matrix environment (Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016b.

claim: Free protons are extremely scarce in an alkaline mitochondrial matrix (~0.4 protons in a mitochondrion of 2 μm length and 200 nm diameter at pH 8.0).
source: Furthermore, free protons are extremely scarce in an alkaline mitochondrial matrix (~0.4 protons in a mitochondrion of 2 μm length and 200 nm diameter at pH 8.0), and matrix pH buffering capacity is estimated to be about 5 mM per pH unit at pH 8.0 (i.e., 1:500,000 for free: bound proton ratio) (Poburko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Poburko et al., 2011.

claim: Matrix pH buffering capacity is estimated to be about 5 mM per pH unit at pH 8.0.
source: Furthermore, free protons are extremely scarce in an alkaline mitochondrial matrix (~0.4 protons in a mitochondrion of 2 μm length and 200 nm diameter at pH 8.0), and matrix pH buffering capacity is estimated to be about 5 mM per pH unit at pH 8.0 (i.e., 1:500,000 for free: bound proton ratio) (Poburko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Poburko et al., 2011.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy has shown nanoscale protein partition of UCP4 and F1Fo-ATP synthase, residing in the inner boundary membrane and the cristae membrane, respectively, in mitochondria from neurons.
source: Consistent with this model, super-resolution microscopy has shown, in the mitochondria from neurons, nanoscale protein partition of UCP4 and F1Fo-ATP synthase, residing in the inner boundary membrane and the cristae membrane, respectively (Klotzsch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klotzsch et al., 2015.

claim: Several groups have independently proposed that F1Fo-ATP synthase is of the same molecular identity as that of mPTP.
source: Several groups have independently proposed that F1Fo-ATP synthase is of the same molecular identity as that of mPTP (Giorgio et al., 2013; Alavian et al., 2014; Bonora et al., 2013; Bernardi et al., 2015), whose flickering openings signify the ignition of mitoflashes (Wang et al., 2008; Hou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Flickering openings of mPTP signify the ignition of mitoflashes.
source: Several groups have independently proposed that F1Fo-ATP synthase is of the same molecular identity as that of mPTP (Giorgio et al., 2013; Alavian et al., 2014; Bonora et al., 2013; Bernardi et al., 2015), whose flickering openings signify the ignition of mitoflashes (Wang et al., 2008; Hou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: UCP2 is the dominant isoform of UCPs in heart.
source: Inhibition of UCP2, the dominant isoform of UCPs in heart (Ricquier and Bouillaud, 2000) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ricquier and Bouillaud, 2000 and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: A Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATPase has been demonstrated in hippocampal neuronal mitochondria.
source: Recently, a Bcl-xL-regulated proton leakage through F1Fo-ATPase has been demonstrated with multiple approaches, including patch-clamping of sub-mitochondrial vesicles, proton flux measurement, and immunochemical demonstration of a Bcl-xL interaction with the β-subunit of ATP synthase in hippocampal neuronal mitochondria (Alavian et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alavian et al., 2011 and Chen et al., 2011b.

claim: Mitoflash activity is a biomarker for mitochondrial energy metabolism under certain conditions.
source: The generation of mitoflashes in intact cells requires the integrity of the electron transfer chain (ETC) (Wang et al., 2008); and mitoflash frequency is highly regulated over a wide dynamic range by factors including metabolic state, thus the mitoflash activity is considered a biomarker for mitochondrial energy metabolism under certain conditions (Wei et al., 2011; Pouvreau, 2010; Fang et al., 2011; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individual mitoflashes occur only intermittently and are confined to single mitochondria.
source: Individual mitoflashes occur only intermittently, and are confined to single mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is based on observations described in the discussion section.

claim: Mitoflashes operate in the frequency-modulatory mode, with relatively constant average amplitude and duration in different conditions.
source: They are digital and operate in the frequency-modulatory mode, i.e, the average amplitude and duration of mitoflashes are relatively constant in different conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on observations described in the discussion section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A cardiac myocyte typically contains 5,000–8,000 mitochondria.
source: In a cardiac myocyte typically containing 5,000–8,000 mitochondria, only a tiny portion of mitochondria undergo the flashing activity at any moment
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: Only a tiny portion of mitochondria undergo the flashing activity at any moment in a cardiac myocyte.
source: In a cardiac myocyte typically containing 5,000–8,000 mitochondria, only a tiny portion of mitochondria undergo the flashing activity at any moment
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed mitoflash frequency and the total number of mitochondria.

claim: ATP diffuses freely in the cytosol.
source: Keeping in mind that ATP diffuses freely in the cytosol, such local, stochastic ATP-negating events afford a novel mechanism to finely regulate ATP homeostasis at the cellular level.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Pyruvate treatment did not induce any changes in cytosolic Ca2+.
source: The lack of significant effect of Ru360 on mitoflashes in cardiomyocytes is expected because pyruvate treatment did not induce any changes in cytosolic Ca2+ and thus mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pyruvate stimulation caused a slight decrease of mitochondrial ROS.
source: Further, electrical pacing did not alter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and pyruvate stimulation caused a slight decrease of mitochondrial ROS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that ROS are unlikely a major player, either.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Electrical pacing did not alter mitochondrial ROS.
source: Further, electrical pacing did not alter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and pyruvate stimulation caused a slight decrease of mitochondrial ROS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that ROS are unlikely a major player, either.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TMRM measurement revealed little effects of pyruvate stimulation, electrical pacing, ISO treatment, and EGTA treatment on ΔΨm.
source: TMRM measurement revealed little effects of these manipulations on ΔΨm, excluding changes in ΔΨm as a possible cause of the mitoflash response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Inhibiting MCU with Ru360 did not show any significant effect on mitoflash frequency.
source: Moreover, inhibiting MCU with Ru360 did not show any significant effect on mitoflash frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mitoflash is sensitive to MCU inhibition in situations when it is induced by elevations of mitochondrial Ca2+.
source: However, mitoflash is sensitive to MCU inhibition in situations when it is induced by elevations of mitochondrial Ca2+, e.g., in HeLa cells under hyperosmotic stress or high cytosolic Ca2+ stimulation (in permeabilized cells) (Hou et al., 2013; Jian et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mitoflashes can serve as a biomarker of mitochondrial respiration when substrate supply is changed and ATP demand is held constant.
source: That mitoflash can serve as the biomarker of mitochondrial respiration is merely a special case when the substrate supply is changed and at the same time the ATP demand is held constant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discussion of mitoflash responses under different conditions.

claim: The bioenergetics-dependent mechanism is more powerful than the Ca2+-dependent mechanism in dominating the mitoflash response in the present experimental conditions.
source: Thus, the bioenergetics-dependent mechanism might be more powerful than the Ca2+-dependent mechanism, thus dominating the mitoflash response in the present experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed mitoflash responses to pacing and Ca2+ manipulations.

claim: Multifaceted energy-consuming processes occur in a mitoflash, including diversion of electrons from energy metabolism to bursting superoxide production, dissipation of ΔΨm, and loss of membrane permeability due to flickering mPTP opening.
source: First of all, multifaceted energy-consuming processes occur in a mitoflash, including diversion of electrons from energy metabolism to bursting superoxide production, dissipation of ΔΨm, and loss of membrane permeability due to flickering mPTP opening (Wang et al., 2008, 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mitochondria undergoing a mitoflash are at a state of futile respiration.
source: All these events indicate that mitochondria undergoing a mitoflash are at a state of futile respiration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed characteristics of mitoflashes.

claim: As ΔμH dissipates during a mitoflash, Complex V could operate in the reverse mode, switching on its ATPase activity and consuming ATP in the flashing mitochondria.
